player.seasonOutlook: The Pelicans made headlines on NBA draft night in 2025 when they traded an unprotected first round pick for Queen. Queen then went out and turned in an impressive rookie season with rounded averages of 12 PPG, 7 RPG and 4 APG in 25 MPG. While the Pelicans have several talented options in the frontcourt, Queen seems to be a big part of their future plans and thus could push for more minutes and opportunity in Year 2. If he gets starter minutes, Queen has nightly double-double potential.

Ware is a prime breakout candidate this season after he was traded to the Bucks as part of the package for Giannis Antetokounmpo. Ware averaged almost a double-double with a 3-pointer, block and steal in about 22 MPG for the Heat last season. His role is expected to be larger in Milwaukee, where he could get near starter minutes in a big man rotation that includes another big with scoring range in Myles Turner. If Ware does get those minutes, he has top-75 upside in points leagues and top-40 in category leagues, where those defensive and 3-point stats are more vital.

Sheppard got major minutes in Year 2, in part due to the injury absence of Fred VanVleet. Sheppard capitalized on those minutes to prove himself a plus shooter-scorer with enough playmaking, rebounding and defense to post positive peripheral numbers. However, VanVleet returns this season and the Rockets brought in Marcus Smart as well. Sheppard still has a key role for the team as a shooter and scorer off the bench, but his fantasy upside may be capped by role and minutes competition.

Wiggins should open the season as Miami’s third option behind Giannis Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo. Playing off those two should give Wiggins more catch-and-shoot opportunities and help his efficiency, but it could also keep his usage modest. A breakout season is unlikely, but replicating last season’s production isn’t out of the realm of possibility. Wiggins is a solid target in the double-digit rounds for managers looking for scoring, threes and rebounds.

Edey enters his third season as one of the more fascinating centers if he can stay healthy. He averaged 13.6 PPG, 11.1 RPG and 1.9 BPG while shooting 63.3% from the field in just 25.8 MPG last season. Memphis went 7-4 in his 11 appearances, and the Grizzlies were plus-18 per 100 possessions with Edey on the floor. The upside is clear, with Edey offering double-double production, strong rebounding and blocks. The concern is durability after another foot surgery. If healthy, Edey has room to take another statistical jump.

Williams is coming off an injury-riddled season in which he was only able to play 33 games at a career-low 28.4 MPG. After an offseason to get healthy, Williams is expected to bounce back to or even surpass the rounded 22 points, 5 rebounds, 5 assists and 2 combined blocks and steals he posted in 2024-25. Still only 25 years old and playing next to Shai Gilgeous-Alexander and Chet Holmgren, Williams should still be getting better every season.

Gordon enters this season looking to stay healthy after injuries limited him to just 36 games last season. He averaged 16.2 PPG, 5.8 RPG and 2.7 APG while shooting 49.7% from the field. Gordon can provide efficient scoring, rebounds and some three-point production, but durability has become a concern after he played only 51 games the previous season. He’s best viewed as a late-round bench stash, with his value tied closely to how many games he can stay on the floor.

Harris enters the season competing with Julian Champagnie for the Spurs starting power forward job. He averaged 13.3 PPG and 5.1 RPG in 63 games for the Pistons last season, then raised his production to 18.1 PPG and 7.2 RPG in the playoffs. Harris brings shooting, rebounding and the ability to create his own shot, but San Antonio’s deep rotation could limit his usage. Winning the starting job would give him a clearer path to fantasy value. Given the circumstances, Harris is worth taking a flier on later in drafts.

Vassell appears to have a smaller offensive role entering this season but remains an important two-way piece for the Spurs. He averaged 13.9 PPG while shooting 38.4% from three last season, despite a 17.6% usage rate. Vassell was even better after the All-Star break, hitting 43.5% from deep. His shooting, shot creation and improved perimeter defense should keep him on the floor, but San Antonio’s crowded rotation limits Vassell’s scoring ceiling. He’s a solid source of triples and efficient scoring near the end of your drafts.

Vucevic was a metronome of double-double production for 13 seasons, averaging a rounded 18 points and 11 rebounds from 2012-13 through 2024-25. Last season, he was traded to the Celtics midseason and saw his minutes and production dip precipitously. Some was due to performance and some to injury, but he was not fantasy viable with the Celtics. This offseason he returned to the Magic and is expected to compete with Wendell Carter Jr. for minutes. He may not get enough time to produce to his typical levels, but if for any reason he gets starter minutes again you can almost pencil his double-double in.

Porzingis is one of the elite per-minute producers of his generation, but injuries have consistently derailed his availability and is already out for training camp. Porzingis missed 50 games last season and 40 the season before, and has missed at least 16 games in nine straight seasons. He is slotted to be the Warriors' starting center this season, and when he plays he will produce, but he is risky to draft in fantasy leagues before the late-middle rounds at the earliest.

Porter had an excellent season on a per-game basis, posting averages similar to his peak season with the Rockets in 2022-23. But he was limited to only 38 games, and had to undergo surgery on his right knee in April. When healthy, Porter will be one of several young guards vying for minutes on the rebuilding Bucks. Porter's production is likely capped by his situation, but if he gets anywhere near starter minutes he has shown he can produce enough to be a viable fantasy option.

Murray enters the season as Sacramento’s likely starting power forward after an injury-plagued fourth season. He averaged 14.0 PPG, 5.7 RPG and 1.6 BPG last season, but shot a career-low 27.7% from three. His defensive production gives him fantasy value even when the shot isn’t falling, while a return to his earlier shooting form would raise his ceiling considerably. Murray still has competition for minutes in Sacramento’s frontcourt, but his two-way role should keep him involved. He’s worth a late-round flier in fantasy drafts.

Demin enters his second season after averaging 10.3 PPG, 3.2 RPG and 3.3 APG while shooting 38.5% from beyond the arc as a rookie. He was even better on catch-and-shoot attempts, hitting 40.5%, and showed more ability to attack the rim and create off the dribble during Summer League. With Mikel Brown Jr. and Julius Randle handling more of the offense, Demin should get a ton of opportunities off the ball. Plantar fasciitis remains a concern, but he’s a player fantasy managers should take a late round flier on if his scoring and playmaking continue to develop.

Grimes arrives in Los Angeles after averaging 13.4 PPG, 3.6 RPG and 3.3 APG in 29.4 MPG for Philadelphia last season. He is expected to have a chance to start alongside Luka Doncic and Austin Reaves, which should create plenty of open looks. His usage could decline, but he’s worth taking a flier late in drafts for managers looking for points and threes.

Green averaged 8.4 PPG, 5.5 RPG and 5.5 APG in 27.5 MPG across 68 appearances. He also made 1.5 triples per game, though Green shot just 32.6% from deep. Steve Kerr wants Green taking more 3-pointers while also cutting down on turnovers after he averaged 2.7 per game last season. Green’s assists, rebounds and defensive stats still provide fantasy value, but his limited scoring keeps him more of a waiver wire option.

Queta is coming off of a breakout season in which he averaged 10.2 PPG, 8.4 RPG and 1.3 BPG in 25.3 MPG while shooting 65.3% from the field. He started 75 of 76 games and emerged as a very good rim protector for Boston. The addition of Mitchell Robinson creates some uncertainty around his playing time, but Queta’s rebounds, blocks and high field goal percentage add to his fantasy appeal. His outlook will depend largely on how Boston divides the center minutes, making him better suited for the waiver wire outside of deeper leagues.

Collin Sexton enters this season as a key scoring option off the Lakers’ bench after averaging 15.4 PPG and 3.3 APG in just 23.7 MPG last season. He shot 48.5% from the field and 40.1% from three, including 44.5% on catch-and-shoot attempts. Sexton can create off the dribble, attack the rim and provide secondary playmaking, but a reserve role behind Luka Doncic and Austin Reaves limits his ceiling. He’s a source of points and triples, but is most likely a waiver wire add unless you are in a deeper league.

Robinson is now with the Celtics after averaging 5.7 PPG, 8.8 RPG and 1.2 BPG in just 19.6 MPG for the Knicks last season. He also grabbed 4.2 offensive RPG, second most in the league, while shooting 72.3% from the field. Robinson can provide rebounds, blocks and a high field goal percentage, but he’ll compete with Neemias Queta for center minutes and remains a poor free throw shooter. Durability is another concern despite playing 60 games last season. He’s best viewed as a waiver wire option for managers looking for rebounds and blocks.

Monk’s role in the rotation is uncertain after averaging 12.5 PPG and 3.0 APG in 22.0 MPG last season. He remained an effective perimeter scorer, shooting 39.5% from beyond the arc and 87.9% from the line, but appeared in only 62 games and made just three starts. Sacramento’s crowded backcourt could make consistent minutes difficult to come by. Monk can still provide scoring, threes and assists when given enough playing time, but he’s best viewed as a waiver-wire option in standard leagues.

Poole enters the season with an uncertain role after a disappointing first season in New Orleans. He averaged 13.4 PPG, 3.1 APG and 2.0 RPG in 23.9 MPG while shooting just 37.2% from the field across 39 appearances. Poole also fell out of the rotation at times, and competition from Dejounte Murray, Jeremiah Fears and Bennedict Mathurin could make consistent minutes difficult to find. He can still provide points, threes and assists when given enough playing time, but he’s best viewed as a waiver-wire option in most leagues.

Pippen Jr. enters the season competing for a significant role in Memphis’ backcourt following the Ja Morant trade. He averaged 11.4 PPG, 4.7 APG and 1.9 SPG in just 21.2 MPG last season, though toe injuries limited him to just 10 games. Pippen has produced when given starter-level minutes, averaging 14.2 PPG and 5.7 APG across 21 starts in 2024-25. Ty Jerome may open the season as the starter, but Pippen’s assists and steals give him intriguing upside.

Johnson was awarded the Sixth Man of the Year while averaging 13.2 PPG and 5.4 RPG in 23.3 minutes per game. He also shot 51.9% from the field while appearing in all 82 games. The concern is playing time after his role shrank during San Antonio’s playoff run, especially with Dylan Harper expected to take on more minutes and Tobias Harris, Julian Champagnie and Carter Bryant competing on the wing. Johnson remains a useful scorer and rebounder, but he’s best viewed as a late round flier in deeper leagues or a waiver-wire option in standard formats.

Grant arrives in Memphis after averaging 18.6 PPG, 3.5 RPG and 2.1 APG while shooting 45.3% from the field with the Blazers last season. He remains a useful source of scoring and threes, but his modest rebounding and assist numbers limit his overall fantasy ceiling. Grant’s role could also fluctuate as the Grizzlies gives significant opportunities to young players like Cameron Boozer and Cedric Coward. He’s best viewed as a waiver wire option in standard leagues.

Wallace enters the season positioned for a larger role after starting 58 of 77 games last season. In those starts, he averaged 9.3 PPG, 3.1 RPG, 2.9 APG and 2.1 SPG. With Luguentz Dort no longer in Oklahoma City, Wallace has a clear path to becoming a full-time starter. His scoring ceiling may be limited, but Wallace’s steals, threes and increased playing time make him an intriguing target at the end of your draft, especially in category leagues.

Sharpe faces a lengthy absence after undergoing surgery to repair the lateral meniscus in his right knee. He averaged 20.8 PPG, 4.3 RPG, 2.6 APG and 1.4 SPG in 50 games last season, but won’t be reevaluated until late February. A March return is possible if his recovery goes well, though there’s no guarantee he’ll be ready by then. Sharpe is difficult to draft in standard leagues, but his scoring upside makes him a worthwhile stash for the 2027-28 season for this in keeper formats.

Henderson’s role this season is uncertain role after averaging 14.2 PPG, 3.7 APG and 2.7 RPG in 24.9 MPG last season. He flashed his upside in the playoffs, including games of 31 and 21 points against San Antonio. The concern is playing time after Portland added Ja Morant to an already crowded backcourt. Henderson still has scoring and playmaking upside, but consistent minutes could be difficult to find.

Jones has a chance to earn a significant role in Chicago’s backcourt after averaging 14.1 PPG, 5.4 APG and 1.2 SPG across 65 games last season. He started 41 games and shot an impressive 55.3% from the field, while his 76 steals led the Bulls. Jones offers assists, steals and efficient scoring, but his 31.5% shooting from three and uncertain role alongside Josh Giddey limit his ceiling. He’s worth a flier, with more upside if he wins a starting job.

Stewart joins the Grizzlies after averaging 10.0 PPG, 5.0 RPG and 1.6 BPG while shooting 55% from the field for the Pistons last season. He also shot 33.3% from beyond the arc on 2.1 attempts per game, giving him some floor-spacing ability. Stewart should have a steady reserve role behind Zach Edey and can play both frontcourt spots. His defense, rebounding and blocks give him some fantasy appeal, but his ceiling depends on minutes.

Filipowski enters his third season after averaging career highs of 11.4 PPG, 7.2 RPG and 2.6 APG across 77 games last season. He can score inside, stretch the floor and contribute as a passer, but Utah’s crowded frontcourt could make consistent minutes difficult to find. Lauri Markkanen, Jaren Jackson Jr., Jusuf Nurkić and Jaxson Hayes are all competing for frontcourt minutes. Filipowski still has intriguing upside, but he’s best viewed as a waiver-wire option in standard formats.

Carrington enters his third season after averaging 10.7 PPG, 4.6 APG and 3.4 RPG while shooting 40.8% from 3 across all 82 games last season. His minutes dipped to 27.7 per game, and Washington’s deeper backcourt could make consistent playing time harder to come by alongside Trae Young and Tre Johnson. Carrington’s shooting and playmaking still give him some upside, but for now he’s best viewed as a waiver-wire option in standard formats.

Mogbo enters the season on a two-way contract with Sacramento after falling out of Toronto’s rotation last season. As a rookie, he averaged 6.2 PPG, 4.9 RPG and 2.3 APG in 20.4 MPG, showing intriguing rebounding and playmaking ability. Mogbo also impressed during Summer League, averaging 11.5 PPG, 8.8 RPG, 2.8 APG and 1.5 BPG. Mogbo could earn opportunities if injuries hit Sacramento’s frontcourt, but for now he’s best viewed as a waiver wire option.
